```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/scout.db")
postings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "scout_postings") |> tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

```{r sql_dplyr}
# Today: dplyr, on the data frame from dbReadTable()
postings |> # pipe = then ; take postings, then
  dplyr::filter(remote == 1) |> # filter by remote jobs, then...; also same as WHERE
  dplyr::count(company, sort = TRUE) |> # count by company; same as doing GROUP BY + COUNT(*) + ORDER BY
  head(10) 

# without count, it will filter and return all of the column names, but count() groups the remaining rows by company and counts the rows
```

```{r}
# can do variable = jobs |>  and set the variable to the output of the query
jobs = postings |>
  dplyr::select(company, title, location_state, remote, category, posted_at, last_seen_at)
jobs

jobs |>
  dplyr::select(company, location_state, remote, posted_at, last_seen_at) |> # changes columns; use select(-column) to drop
  dplyr::filter(remote == 1) |> # changes rows where a test is TRUE
  dplyr::mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as.Date(last_seen_at) - as.Date(posted_at))) |> # mutate creates new column, which this creates a column that says how many days the posting has been open for
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(days_open)) |> # changes order; sort by one or more columns; desc() for largest first
  dplyr::group_by(company) |>
  dplyr::summarize(n = dplyr::n(), avg_days = mean(days_open)) # can use count() as a shortcut for n(), but would do summarize as also need to calculate mean
```

# Answering the question about data types

```{r}
jobs = postings |>
  dplyr::select(company, location_state, remote, posted_at, last_seen_at) |>
  dplyr::filter(remote == 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    posted_at = as.Date(posted_at), # force change the column into date format
    last_seen_at = as.Date(last_seen_at),
    days_open = as.numeric(last_seen_at - posted_at)
    ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(days_open)) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(company) |>
  dplyr::summarize(n = dplyr::n(), avg_days = mean(days_open))
```


### select()

```{r select}
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/scout.db")
postings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "scout_postings") |> tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

jobs = postings |>
  dplyr::select(company, title, location_state, remote, category, posted_at, last_seen_at)
jobs
```

### filter()

```{r filter}
c(one_test = jobs |> dplyr::filter(remote == 1) |> nrow(),
  both     = jobs |> dplyr::filter(remote == 1, location_state == "OH") |> nrow(),
  either   = jobs |> dplyr::filter(remote == 1 | category == "internship") |> nrow(),
  in_set   = jobs |> dplyr::filter(location_state %in% c("OH", "IN", "KY")) |> nrow()) # %in% tests membership in a set

# can use is.na() to test for empty cell
# column names don't go in quotations
```

### mutate()

```{r mutate}
# newnew = expression once per row from that row's cells

jobs = jobs |>
  dplyr::mutate(days_open = as.numeric(as.Date(last_seen_at) - as.Date(posted_at)))

jobs |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(days_open)) |> dplyr::select(company, title, days_open)
```

#### Section Helpers and across()

```{r section_helpers}
dplyr::starts_with("location") # names that begin with the text; dplyr::ends_with() and dplyr::contains() work the same way

dplyr::any_of(c("price", "beds")) # these names, if present; no error when one is missing

dplyr::where(is.numeric) # every column of a type; dplyr::everything() is all remaining columns

dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("_at"), as.Date) # inside mutate() or summarize(): one function applied to every matching column
# lets you apply the same function to multiple columns at once

dplyr::if_any(c(title, company), is.na) # inside filter(): one test over several columns
```

```{r across}
jobs = jobs |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("_at"), as.Date))    # both dates at once
jobs |> dplyr::summarize(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), mean))
```

```{r across2}
# without across
postings |>
  dplyr::group_by(company) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    avg_salary = mean(salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_bonus = mean(bonus, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# with across
postings |>
  dplyr::group_by(company) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    dplyr::across(
      c(salary, bonus), # applies the mean function across multiple columns
      mean,
      na.rm = TRUE # ignore missing values
    )
  )
```

### group_by & summarize

```{r group_summarize}
jobs |>
  dplyr::group_by(location_state) |>
  dplyr::summarize(postings = dplyr::n(), remote_share = mean(remote)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(postings))
```


### joins

```{r joins}
states = tibble::tibble(location_state = state.abb,
                        state_name = state.name,
                        region = as.character(state.region))

# the key: location_state holds the same values, meaning the same thing, in both tables
by_state |> dplyr::left_join(states, by = "location_state")    # keep every row on the left
by_state |> dplyr::inner_join(states, by = "location_state")   # keep only the matches
by_state |> dplyr::anti_join(states, by = "location_state")    # keep only the non-matches


# join practice

jobs |>
  dplyr::left_join(states, by = "location_state") |>
  dplyr::group_by(region) |>
  dplyr::summarize(postings = dplyr::n(), remote_share = mean(remote)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(postings))


jobs |> dplyr::count(location_state) |> dplyr::anti_join(states, by = "location_state")

```

dplyr::left_join() - all left rows; NA where no match
dplyr::inner_join() - matches only
dplyr::anti_join() - left rows with no match
dplyr::full_join() - everything from both sides

When the key has different names, by = c("location_state" = "abb").




## Demo

```{r}
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/scout.db")
postings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "scout_postings") |> tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

jobs = postings |>
  dplyr::select(company, title, location_state, remote, category, posted_at, last_seen_at) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("_at"), as.Date),
                days_open = as.numeric(last_seen_at - posted_at))
```

```{r q1_by_category}
# which category is remote friendly
# to answer that, the logic would be as follows:
# - find number of jobs per category
# - normalize the number of remote jobs per category by dividing by the total jobs

jobs |> 
  # I want to move from unit of analysis being a job posting to a category
  dplyr::group_by(category) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    postings= dplyr::n(),
    remote_share = mean(remote)
  ) 
```


```{r q2_by_state}
jobs |> 
  dplyr::group_by(category, location_state) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    postings = dplyr::n(),
    remote_share = mean(remote) |>  round(digits = 2)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(remote_share)) |> 
  na.omit() # drop the location_state == NA and other other rows that contain NA
```


# notes logic for q2

```{r q2_by_state_notes}
jobs |>

```


```{r practice}
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/midwest_airbnb.db")
listings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "listings") |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
dplyr::glimpse(listings)
```


```{r airbnb}
# 1. how many listings per city
## if answer is purely based on last class, i can group by city and then count the number of listings in each city

listings |>  
  dplyr::group_by(city) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(count = dplyr::n())

## alternatively, shortcut for code above

listings |> 
  dplyr::count(city) # count does group by and then n()

## other option is to simply count the number of times each city occured in the col city
table(listings$city) # returns a named vector vs above dataframe/tibble



# 2.For entire homes (room_type == "Entire home/apt") that sleep four or more, what is the median price in each city?

listings |> 
  dplyr::filter(
    room_type == "Entire home/apt" & accommodates >= 4
  ) |> 
  dplyr::group_by(city) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(median_price = median(price))



# 3. Add price_per_person = price / accommodates. Which three listings are cheapest per person? Believe them?

listings |> 
  dplyr::mutate(price_per_person = price / accommodates) |> 
  dplyr::select(city, host_name, name, price, accommodates, price_per_person) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(price_per_person) |> 
  head(3) # tail(3) shows back 3


# 4. Which five host_names have the most listings?
## host_names are not unique, but host_ids are

listings |> 
  dplyr::count(host_name, sort = T)

listings |> 
  dplyr::count(host_name, host_id, sort = T) # now groups by host_name and host_id to separate non-unique host names

## both answers would have been considered correct on the exam given how the question was framed

```
